 A 3.6% Social Security COLA Sounds Like Good News. Here’s the Blow Retirees Won’t See Coming
 Maurie Backman Sat, November 14, 2026 at 4:06 AM CST 4 min read Quick Read 
 The 2027 Social Security COLA of 4% adds roughly $75 to typical monthly checks, but a bigger raise signals heavier inflation pressure on seniors. 
 COLAs look backward at July through September inflation, so rising prices can erase the raise, as happened when inflation surged after 2026's increase. 
 Retirees can strengthen finances by earning extra income through part-time or gig work, or by renting out spare space like a basement or garage. 
 Americans who work with a financial advisor have saved more than twice as much for retirement, on average. Find out what one could change for you: SmartAsset's free quiz matches you with up to three vetted fiduciary advisors in about five minutes. (Sponsor) 
 When the Social Security Administration announced last year that benefits would be getting a 2.8% COLA for 2026, many seniors weren't happy. This year's COLA announcement went differently. 
 brizmaker / Shutterstock.com The 2027 Social Security COLA has been locked in at 3.6%, and that's a much more generous raise for seniors to look forward to. It also means the typical Social Security recipient should see a roughly $75 boost to their monthly checks starting in January. 
 But while a 3.6% Social Security COLA might seem like good news initially, there's a big drawback seniors should know about. 
 Larger COLAs mean more rampant inflation 
 Social Security COLAs are designed to help benefits keep pace with inflation. They're measured by year-over-year changes in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers. 
 The larger any given COLA is, the more inflation has been pounding consumers. And seniors on Social Security often bear the brunt of it, largely because they tend to spend a lot on healthcare, which tends to rise faster than inflation. 
 Not only is a 3.6% Social Security COLA an indication of problematic inflation, but it also does not guarantee that benefits will be able to keep up with inflation in the new year. 
 Social Security COLAs are backward-facing. They're based on previous inflation readings, not current or future ones. 
 ------ 
 Can You Answer These Three Questions? 
 Americans say they need $1.46 million to retire comfortably. Whether that number fits your life depends on three questions most people never work through: 
 1. How much can you withdraw each year without running out? 
 2. When should you claim Social Security? 
 3. How much will taxes take from your 401(k) or IRA?

 In other words, a 3.6% COLA reflects what inflation looked like during the months of July, August, and September. It doesn't tell us what inflation will look like in the coming year. If inflation picks up even more, to the point where it's up 4% year over year, seniors' 3.6% COLA will be rendered fairly useless. 
 Of course, that's not guaranteed to happen. But it happened in 2026. 
 Seniors saw their benefits increase 2.8% at the start of the year, and inflation began surging shortly after in the wake of the Middle East conflict. So it's hard to know what the new year has in store as far as costs go. 
 Don't bank on a 3.6% COLA too heavily 
 If you're on Social Security, you may be hoping that your 3.6% COLA improves your buying power and makes your financial situation better. In reality, that raise may have a limited impact. 
 If you're looking to improve your finances, you're better off taking matters into your own hands. You could consider getting a job and using the money to supplement your Social Security checks. If a steady part-time job doesn't appeal to you, join the gig economy and work when it's convenient. That could mean a few evenings a week or select weekends when you aren't busy. 
 If you don't want to work or can't manage a job but own a home with a separate area, such as a finished basement or garage, renting that space out may be feasible, allowing you to boost your income. 
 It's natural to be happy about a larger Social Security COLA. Just recognize that your raise not only comes at the expense of higher prices, but that it's not guaranteed to hold up well if prices keep soaring.
